insights.headline: Precision and craftsmanship are sacred—quality is worth preserving for decades.
insights.explanation: You've kept and regularly checked Walt's micrometer for 40+ years, verifying it remains 'dead on' despite being passed down in a box after his death. This isn't casual nostalgia; it's active stewardship. The tool and the standard it represents matter enough to maintain.

insights.headline: You honor people by continuing their practice, not through words but through work.
insights.explanation: Walt's death is mentioned factually, almost sparely. But his legacy lives in your hands—literally in how you hold the micrometer, three clicks, letting the tool do the work. You've internalized his method as a living memorial.

insights.headline: The best instruction is economical, respectful, and demonstrated—not explained.
insights.explanation: You emphasize that Walt was silent for four months, then showed you once: 'He didn't say it mean. He just set it down.' You've clearly absorbed his belief that right practice speaks louder than justification, and that restraint is a form of respect.

insights.headline: You have a natural gift for precision work and learning through careful observation.
insights.explanation: You absorbed a technical technique so thoroughly that you've maintained it as gospel for four decades. You don't describe struggle—you describe Walt showing you, and you getting it. That's mastery through attentiveness, not brute effort.

insights.headline: You may process grief and loss through continued precision work rather than emotional expression.
insights.explanation: Walt dies in September, gone by Thanksgiving—you state it factually. But the response is to preserve his tool with exacting care and still verify its accuracy decades later. The work becomes the memorial. Consider whether this pattern serves you in other losses.

insights.headline: You hold onto established ways of doing things, even when the world (and shops) move on.
insights.explanation: The shop closed in '87, but you still maintain a 1980s tool by a 1980s standard. This loyalty to proven methods is a strength—it's why that micrometer is still perfect. But it may also limit your openness to new approaches.

insights.headline: Duty and completion are non-negotiable, even during life's defining moments.
insights.explanation: He left his son's birth to finish 11 remaining parts because of an impending deadline. His own words—'Because if you're gonna do it you do it'—reveal that commitment to completion is his core principle, overriding even the pull of witnessing his child's entry into the world.

insights.headline: He holds himself to high personal standards of quality and integrity, independent of recognition.
insights.explanation: He refused to let a colleague's poor work result in scrapped parts, owning the quality personally. His note that 'it's your name on the traveler' suggests he carries standards not because others demand it, but because his own reputation and integrity demand it.

insights.headline: He is a skilled hands-on maker who can envision and execute complex technical projects with patience.
insights.explanation: He built a functional steel tractor from scrap, complete with broached keyways and turning wheels, over three weeks of lunch breaks. This combines technical skill, spatial reasoning, material knowledge, and sustained commitment to something with no immediate reward.

insights.headline: He finds meaning and purpose in transforming constraint into creation.
insights.explanation: He couldn't give a newborn a nine-pound steel toy, so he built it anyway and preserved it on a shelf as a legacy. This suggests he naturally works within practical limitations and finds lasting solutions within them.

insights.headline: Love means respecting what the moment requires, not forcing emotional gestures.
insights.explanation: He made an elaborate gift for his newborn but understood he couldn't give it to a baby, so he kept it preserved instead. This reflects emotional maturity: care expressed through what's actually appropriate, not what feels sentimentally satisfying.

insights.headline: Work excellence and providing for family are inseparable parts of the same responsibility.
insights.explanation: He returned to finish those 11 parts immediately after his son's birth, suggesting he doesn't see work and fatherhood as competing obligations. Finishing the job is how he shows up for his family.

insights.headline: He processes major life events through quiet action and creation rather than reflection or emotional expression.
insights.explanation: His account of his son's birth is matter-of-fact; no description of feelings or wonder. Instead, he channels that significance into building a tractor over three weeks. This pattern of moving toward making rather than into feeling shapes how he integrates profound moments.

insights.headline: He carries standards of quality and integrity largely alone, without apparent expectation of recognition.
insights.explanation: He manages completion and precision without complaint, aware his colleagues cannot match his standards. Worth exploring: whether this independence flows from quiet pride and self-reliance, or from feeling isolated in his standards—and if he's carrying more than necessary.

insights.headline: Fairness and equity matter more than self-protection, even in crisis.
insights.explanation: His insistence on being fair to his ex-wife—splitting costs, letting her keep the house, refusing to make her a villain—shows fairness isn't conditional. He prioritizes an honest account over a self-serving narrative.

insights.headline: Responsibility to care persists long after the relationship formally ends.
insights.explanation: Years after the divorce, he's fixing her furnace, changing her car's tires, doing it quietly and early so she won't feel obligated. This reveals a core belief that commitment to another person's wellbeing doesn't expire with paperwork.

insights.headline: Reading situations clearly and moving with quiet decisiveness rather than drama.
insights.explanation: He didn't wait for a confrontation—he saw which way things were pointed and took clean action. This pattern of accurate perception and decisive response appears throughout: knowing the furnace fix, timing the snow tires before salt trucks.

insights.headline: Delivering skilled, practical care invisibly—showing up, solving problems, and disappearing.
insights.explanation: His mastery shines through meticulous detail (flame sensors, furniture construction) paired with deliberate invisibility: leaving before she gets home, arriving early before dawn. He's exceptionally comfortable with competence that goes unwitnessed.

insights.headline: Divorce doesn't require enemies—it can be handled fairly and with dignity.
insights.explanation: The straightforward description of splitting costs and letting her keep the house reflects a belief that separation is a change in relationship structure, not a betrayal. This shaped how he moved through the entire experience.

insights.headline: Manhood means staying present and helpful to those who mattered, regardless of status.
insights.explanation: Continuing to care for his ex-wife and showing up consistently for his son suggests he defines himself by what he does, not by the relationship category. He just keeps showing up.

insights.headline: Emotional weight is carried quietly, sometimes without acknowledgment.
insights.explanation: The Christmas Eve moment—sitting in the truck, radio on—is mentioned almost as an afterthought, as if the significance slipped out unexpectedly. This pattern suggests difficulty sitting with or expressing vulnerable feelings directly.

insights.headline: Relational and emotional needs are met through practical action rather than conversation.
insights.explanation: He shows love and care through fixing furnaces and changing tires, appearing early, disappearing quietly. It's worth exploring whether he's comfortable with more direct emotional intimacy or expression.

insights.headline: You need absolute control over your own life, even when it puts you at serious risk.
insights.explanation: Signing yourself out of the hospital against medical advice after a heart attack with 90% blockage isn't just stubbornness—it's a statement about autonomy. You're willing to accept physical danger to maintain self-determination. This shows independence is a core value, perhaps your core value.

insights.headline: You solve problems through action and pragmatism, not reflection or emotional processing.
insights.explanation: You drove yourself to the hospital, got the stent, came home, ate a sandwich, got a battery. You move through crises with efficiency and focus on concrete next steps. This pragmatism keeps you functional, but it may keep you from understanding deeper patterns.

insights.headline: You stay remarkably calm and clear-headed under life-threatening pressure.
insights.explanation: Most people would panic having a heart attack; you drove yourself, stayed lucid enough to watch your own stent placement, made deliberate decisions. This composure under extreme stress is a genuine strength—it's also why you survived.

insights.headline: You believe admitting vulnerability or need is a sign of weakness to be avoided.
insights.explanation: The turkey sandwich detail isn't random—it's evidence that 'everything's fine.' You minimize a life-threatening event to protect yourself from feeling helpless or dependent. This belief keeps you functional but also keeps you isolated.

insights.headline: You assume that sharing difficult truths with people you're close to will create unnecessary conflict.
insights.explanation: Eight months before telling your son about a cardiac event, and even then only by accident. When he reacted emotionally, you didn't engage—you just observed his behavior. This suggests you don't expect people to handle your real struggles well.

insights.headline: You avoid difficult conversations with the people closest to you until circumstances force them.
insights.explanation: Major life events get buried and only surface accidentally months later. This pattern likely limits your relationships and leaves unresolved tension (like with your son's reaction to the heart attack).

insights.headline: You follow through on practical self-care but abandon medical guidance without consulting your doctor.
insights.explanation: You got the battery replaced immediately when you noticed the issue, but you quit medication that had side effects without calling—you just handled it yourself. This suggests you trust your own judgment over expertise when following through requires admitting something isn't working.

insights.headline: He measures his worth through the quality and precision of everything he does
insights.explanation: From cleaning a workstation 'so that's what they remember' after 34 years, to turning a cork grip himself, to recognizing Devon needed precision instruments—this person has built a life around doing things right. The standard is internal and uncompromising.

insights.headline: He believes in helping others without acknowledgment or allowing them to feel indebted
insights.explanation: He gifted Devon a $190 tool set by creating a plausible lie about company inventory, then left before the farewell party. His kindness is designed to be invisible because he values the recipient's dignity more than being thanked.

insights.headline: He has rare practical mastery and an instinct for developing potential in others
insights.explanation: Forty-one years of expertise in precision measurement and machining, skilled enough to build a fly rod from components, perceptive enough to see 'good hands' in Devon despite his technical gaps. He knows how to transfer knowledge quietly.

insights.headline: His sense of purpose and self has been almost entirely defined by his job
insights.explanation: The most striking moment is 'I get up the same time... Then I don't know.' His body keeps the ritual of work, but the meaning is gone. After 41 years, he hasn't built a parallel identity to step into, leaving him untethered.

insights.headline: He manages pain and potential rejection by exiting situations before they can fully form
insights.explanation: He took the buyout before the layoff list was released (so 'I don't know if I was on it'), left at 11:40 before the 2 PM farewell party, exited through the side by the compressor room. He shapes the narrative by leaving rather than being left.

insights.headline: His deepest care for others comes out in practical, handmade gestures, but he seems uncertain it will be received
insights.explanation: He built Nick a custom fly rod with personal details—green wraps for his hockey colors—and finished it with real craftsmanship. Yet he says 'He's in at Christmas. I'll see,' expressing doubt about whether his son will appreciate the gift or whether they'll genuinely connect.

insights.headline: He believes in taking what's his, then letting go without complaint or bitterness
insights.explanation: 'There's probably three hundred dollars of my own tooling in that shop still, which, fine.' He doesn't demand recompense, doesn't cling to what he's lost. This stoicism is admirable but might prevent him from advocating for his own needs or asking for support.
